turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Hey, thanks for joining us. So, we're working on a website called QONYS. It's basically a platform where people can find apartments in new buildings. And we also want to understand how developers work with apartment information. Is it okay if I take some notes?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, sure. That's fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Great. Nothing too formal. Just tell me how things usually work at your company.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Okay, no problem.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, let's start with your job. What exactly do you do?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Well, I'm a sales manager at a development company here in Astana. I've been working there for almost two years now.

Mostly, I talk to customers, answer questions about apartments, explain prices, and help people choose something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, so you work directly with buyers?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, pretty much every day. I also check which apartments are available or already reserved.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you manage information on the website too?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Not directly. We have a marketing team for that. But if I notice something wrong, like an old price or incorrect apartment status, I tell them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, and how does that work? Like, imagine you have a new building. How does all the information get to the website?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, usually we have an Excel file with all the apartments. It has apartment numbers, floors, areas, prices, and statuses.

Then our marketing team takes that information and adds it to the website.

The floor plans and building pictures usually come from our architects or designers.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So everything is in one place?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
No, that's actually one of the problems. Prices are in one file, plans are in another folder, and pictures are somewhere else.

Sometimes it's a bit messy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you give me an example?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah. Let's say we have apartment 45 on the sixth floor. In Excel, it's easy to find. But the floor plan might have some strange file name, like "floor6_final_v2."

Then someone has to open it and check if it's actually the correct plan.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Sounds like extra work.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. Especially when you have hundreds of apartments.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, and what about prices? Let's say an apartment gets reserved or the price changes. What happens?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Usually, the sales department updates our apartment list, and then the information needs to be updated on the website.

But sometimes there's a delay.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that caused any problems before?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, actually. I remember one situation when an apartment was already reserved, but the website still showed it as available.

A customer called and asked about it. I had to explain that it wasn't available anymore.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what did he say?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
He wasn't very happy. He said something like, "But it's still available on your website."

And, well, he was right.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you handle it?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I apologised and offered him another apartment on a similar floor. But he didn't really like that one.

So, yeah, we probably lost that customer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would help avoid situations like that?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I think prices and availability should be updated in one place. And the website should show the new information quickly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Let's say your company starts selling apartments in a new building. What information do you need first?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
First, basic things. Building name, location, number of floors, completion date, and some general information about the project.

Then we need the apartment list, prices, floor plans, and pictures.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is all of that usually ready at the same time?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
No, not really. Sometimes the sales information is ready, but the marketing team is still preparing pictures.

Or we have the building pictures, but some apartment plans are not final yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what do you do in that situation?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
We just wait or prepare what we can.

I think it would be convenient if we could add the information step by step. Like, save the project as a draft and publish it when everything important is ready.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you want to check it before publishing?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. Especially apartment numbers and prices. Those mistakes can cause real problems.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, let's talk about customers. What do they usually ask about apartment prices and finishing?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Oh, finishing is a common question.

A lot of people ask about WhiteBox or rough finishing. Some customers don't really understand the difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, I've heard those words too. How do you explain them?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I usually explain what's included. Like, what has already been done and what the customer still needs to finish.

Because just saying "WhiteBox" doesn't explain much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And can customers choose a different finishing option?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Depends on the project. Some buildings have only one option. Others let you choose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that change the price?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, sometimes quite a lot.

And that's another thing. People see one price online, but they don't always understand that finishing or furniture might cost extra.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So how would you prefer to show it?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I think just show the total price for each available option.

Like, this is the price without finishing, and this is the price with finishing. Simple.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And who usually prepares the building images and floor plans?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: The architects make the original plans, and our design team prepares the images for the website.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about those interactive plans where you can click on a floor or an apartment?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, I've seen those. They're useful, actually.

You can choose a floor and see which apartments are available.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it difficult to prepare something like that?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I don't do it myself, but I think connecting all the apartments correctly takes time.

And someone definitely needs to check it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Well, imagine you click on apartment 35 and it opens apartment 36. The customer might not even notice the mistake at first.

Then they call us about the wrong apartment. It's confusing for everyone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you'd want to check the clickable areas?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah. If the system could help prepare them, that would be great. But I still think someone from our team should check them before publishing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, let's say someone finds an apartment on your website and sends a request. What happens next?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Usually, we receive their phone number, and one of our managers calls them.

Sometimes we also receive messages through WhatsApp.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you know which apartment they're interested in?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Not always. That's actually annoying sometimes.

We get a phone number, call the person, and then have to ask what building they're looking at and which apartment they liked.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What information would you want to receive?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
At least the building name, apartment number, floor, and price.

If they selected a finishing option, that would be useful too.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And how do you keep track of all the requests?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
We have our own system and sometimes use spreadsheets. But it's not always convenient.

It would be nice to see which requests are new and which ones someone has already answered.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has it happened that two managers called the same person?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, a few times. It's not a big disaster, but it doesn't look very professional.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, now let's imagine you're using our website. You need to add a building, check its floor plans, and answer a customer request. Where would you start?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, okay. I'd probably open something like "My Developments."

Then I'd choose the building I want to work with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, and what would you do next?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd look for a way to upload apartment information. Ideally from Excel, because we already have all that data.

Then I'd add the building pictures and floor plans.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And how would you check the plans?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I'd choose a floor, click on a few apartments, and see if the apartment numbers and information are correct.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about customer requests?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd open the requests section and check the newest ones first.

It would be good to see which apartment each customer selected.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that's unclear or missing?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, one thing. I would want to know whether a change becomes public immediately or if I have to publish it again.

Because if I just change one apartment price, I don't want to go through ten different steps.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Anything else?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, uploading many apartments at once. If I had to enter 200 apartments manually, I probably wouldn't use it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, last main question. What would make your team actually want to use a platform like this?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I think it has to save time. That's the main thing.

If we can update prices, upload apartments, and manage customer requests in one place, that's useful.

But if we have to do the same work in two different systems, people won't like it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about features like 360-degree views of the building or courtyard?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I think they're good for customers. Sometimes people call and ask what the courtyard looks like or what's around the building.

If they could see it themselves, that might save us some questions.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would it be difficult for your team to work with?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Well, depends. If we can just upload ready 360-degree pictures, that's fine.

But if we need to build some complicated 3D model for every project, that's probably too much work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what would be the biggest reason not to use QONYS?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Probably if it's too complicated. We already have enough work.

I don't want to spend half my day just updating the website.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text:
Okay, I think that's everything. So, from what I understood, one of your biggest problems is keeping apartment information updated, especially prices and availability.

And the second thing is that you want a simple way to upload information and manage customer requests without doing extra work. Is that right?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. That's pretty much it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything else we missed?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Hmm, maybe mobile support. Sometimes I'm not at my computer, so checking requests from my phone would be useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, makes sense. Thanks a lot for your time.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: No problem. Good luck with the project!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Hey, thanks for joining us. So, we're making a website called QONYS. It helps people find apartments in new buildings. We just want to talk about your experience looking for an apartment. Is it okay if I take notes?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, sure. No problem.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Great. Nothing complicated, just tell me how it was for you.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Okay, sounds good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, have you been looking for an apartment recently?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, kind of. I'm 22, still studying at university, but I also work part-time. I've been thinking about getting my own apartment in Astana.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh, nice. Are you planning to buy one soon?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Well, not right now. Probably in the next year or two. I'm saving money, and my parents might help a little.

But I wanted to start looking now, you know, just to understand the prices and see what's available.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what kind of apartment do you want?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Probably a two-room apartment. Maybe a big one-room apartment if it's in a really good location.

My girlfriend and I have been looking at some options together.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you're planning to live there yourself?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. I just want a comfortable place that's not too far from work and the city centre.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, and where did you start? Like, what was the first website you opened?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Krisha.kz, obviously. I think everyone uses it.

I just selected Astana, chose my budget, and started looking at apartments.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you find anything interesting?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, a few apartments. But then I wanted to see more details, so I opened the developers' websites.

Some were okay, but others were pretty confusing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Confusing how?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Well, sometimes you see a nice picture of a building, but it's difficult to find the actual apartments and their prices.

Like, I don't want to read five pages about the building. I just want to see what's available.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you use maps too?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, mostly 2GIS. I checked how far the buildings were from my university and work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, what's the most important thing for you? Price, location, size?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, probably price first. My budget is around 30 million tenge.

I know it's not a huge budget, but I'm trying to find something good.

Location is important too. I don't want to spend an hour getting to work every morning.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the floor or apartment size?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'm not that picky about the floor. I mean, I wouldn't really want the first floor, but other than that, it's fine.

For size, I would prefer two rooms, but I could also choose a large one-room apartment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what would make you reject an apartment?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Probably if it's too expensive or really far away.

Also, if the layout is strange. Like, a huge corridor and a tiny kitchen. I don't really see the point of that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, when you found a few apartments you liked, what did you do with them?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Honestly, I just sent links to my girlfriend on WhatsApp.

Sometimes I took screenshots too.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And how did you compare them?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Well, we opened the links and looked at the prices and plans.

But after a while, it got confusing. I had a lot of screenshots, and I didn't remember which apartment was from which developer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Haha, yeah. Did you try making a list or something?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, I tried using my phone notes.

I wrote down prices and areas, but I stopped after a few apartments. It was just annoying to update everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would make that easier?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Maybe a way to save apartments and compare them directly.

Like, choose three apartments and see their prices, sizes, floors, and plans next to each other.

I think that would be much easier.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you contact any developers to check apartment prices?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, I called two of them.

One apartment looked really good. It was around 28 million tenge, if I remember correctly.

But when I called, the manager said it wasn't available anymore.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh, really? Was it still on the website?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, that's why I called. It still showed the apartment as available.

The manager offered me another one, but it was more expensive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That's annoying. What about finishing options? Did you check those?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, but at first I didn't really understand them.

Like, I saw apartments with WhiteBox finishing, but I didn't know exactly what that included.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What did you think it meant?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I thought the apartment was almost ready to live in.

But then I found out that I'd still need to spend money on some finishing work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So was that a problem for your budget?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, definitely. Because if I buy an apartment for 30 million and then need a few million more for repairs, that's a big difference.

I'd prefer to see the full cost before contacting anyone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, and how did you understand where the apartment was located in the building?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Mostly from the floor plans.

But sometimes I could only see the rooms. I couldn't understand which side of the building the apartment was on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And why was that important to you?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Well, I wanted to know where the windows faced.

Like, if the windows face a busy road, it might be noisy. And if they face the courtyard, that could be nicer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did the building pictures help?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
A little, but not really. Most of them were just nice pictures of the whole building.

I couldn't understand where my actual apartment was.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about a 360-degree view of the courtyard or the building? Would that help?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, I think so. It would be pretty cool to look around and see the area from different points.

Especially if I could see the courtyard, parking, and nearby buildings.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would that replace visiting the building?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
No, probably not. I'd still want to go there myself before buying.

But it would help me decide which buildings are worth visiting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, when you contacted those developers, how did it go?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Mostly fine. I left my phone number on one website, and the manager called me back.

He explained the apartment and asked when I wanted to visit their sales office.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you go?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: No, not yet. I told him I was just checking options for the future.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And was he okay with that?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, but he called me again a few days later.

And then another time.

I mean, I understand it's his job, but I wasn't ready to buy anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what would be a better way to contact developers?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I think sending a message would be easier.

Like, I choose an apartment, ask my question, and the manager answers.

I don't mind giving my name and phone number if I'm seriously interested.

But I don't want to register or share too much information just to look at prices.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: By the way, what language do you normally use on these websites?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Mostly Russian. I'm just used to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about Kazakh?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I understand Kazakh too. But sometimes the Russian version of a website has more information.

So I usually stay on the Russian version.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were there any words you didn't understand?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, WhiteBox was one of them. Also, some descriptions used construction terms I didn't know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What did you do when you saw those words?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I just Googled them.

But I think it would be easier if the website explained everything in simple words.

Maybe show some pictures of what the apartment looks like with each finishing option.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, now let's look at our website. Imagine you're searching for your first apartment here. What would you do first?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Okay, let me see.

Hmm, first I'd probably set my budget. Let's say 30 million.

Then I'd choose one-room and two-room apartments.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What next?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd probably check the map. I want something close to work or at least near public transport.

Then I'd open a building that looks interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And how would you choose an apartment inside the building?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd check the available floors and open a floor plan.

Oh, that's useful. I can actually see where the apartment is located.

Then I'd check the price and area.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Let's say you find another apartment you like. What would you do?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd want to compare them.

Like, see which one is cheaper, which one has a better layout, and which one is in a better location.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And if you decided to contact the developer?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd probably use the contact button and ask whether the apartment is still available.

Maybe ask about the final price too.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that's unclear here?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, maybe the finishing options. I'd like to see what exactly changes when I choose another option.

And I think the full price should be really clear.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Anything else?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Maybe a way to save apartments without creating an account immediately.

Because sometimes I just want to look around.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, last question. Imagine you could just describe what apartment you want to an AI assistant, and it finds some options for you. Would you try that?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. I think that sounds useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you tell it?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, something like, "Find me a two-room apartment in Astana under 30 million tenge, near public transport."

Maybe I'd also say I want a modern building and a good kitchen.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And would you trust what it suggests?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Well, I'd check everything myself first.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you check?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
The price, location, and floor plan.

Because AI can make mistakes, right?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, that's possible. What would make the suggestions more useful?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
If it explained why it selected each apartment.

Like, "This apartment is within your budget and close to a bus stop."

That would be nice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And if you could choose just one feature to make your apartment search easier, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, probably comparing apartments.

Because right now I have to open ten different websites just to compare a few options.

If everything was in one place, that would save a lot of time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text:
Okay, I think that's everything. Let me just check if I understood you correctly.

So, you're looking for your first apartment, but you're not planning to buy immediately.

Your biggest problems are comparing different apartments and understanding the real total price, especially when finishing isn't included. Right?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, exactly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And you think interactive floor plans, maps, and an AI assistant could make the search easier.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah. Especially if the website is simple and I don't have to open a lot of other pages.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything else you want to add?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Hmm, not really. Maybe just make it work well on phones. I usually search for apartments on my phone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, makes sense. Thanks a lot for your time!

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: No problem. Good luck!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Hey, thanks for joining. So, we're working on a website called QONYS. It helps people find apartments in new buildings. We just want to hear about your experience looking for an apartment. Is it okay if I take some notes?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, sure. No problem.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Great. There are no right or wrong answers, so just tell me how it was for you.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Okay, sounds good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, have you been looking for an apartment recently?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, actually. I've been looking for a few months now. I'm thinking about buying an apartment in Astana, but not for myself. I want to rent it out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh, okay. So it's more like an investment?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. I work full-time, and I've saved some money. I thought buying a small apartment could be a good investment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what kind of apartment do you want?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Probably a one-room apartment. Maybe a studio, I'm not sure yet. I just want something that's not too expensive and would be easy to rent out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, and where did you start? Like, what was the first thing you did?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I started with Krisha.kz. I think that's where most people start. I checked prices in different areas and looked at some new residential complexes.

Then I opened a few developers' websites to see more information.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you use anything else?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, mostly 2GIS. I wanted to see what's around the buildings. Like bus stops, universities, shopping centres, things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why universities?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Well, I think an apartment near a university could be easier to rent out. Students and young people might be interested. But I'd still need to check the demand.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, what do you care about most? Price, location, size?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd say price and location. My budget is around 30 million tenge, maybe a little more if the apartment is really good.

I don't need a big apartment. For renting, I think a smaller apartment in a good location can be better than a big one somewhere far away.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So the number of rooms doesn't matter that much?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Not really. One room is fine. I care more about how much I spend and how much I could get from rent.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what would make you say no to an apartment?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Hmm, probably a bad location or a very high price. Also, if the apartment needs too much work, I'd have to think about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you found a few apartments you liked, how did you compare them?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Honestly, it was kind of messy. I had like ten tabs open in my browser.

I also saved some screenshots and sent links to myself on Telegram.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Haha, okay. And was that enough?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Not really. After a few days, I couldn't remember which apartment was which.

Like, one apartment was 28 million, another was 30 million, but the second one had better finishing. So I had to open everything again to compare.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would make that easier?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Just putting them next to each other, you know? Price, area, location, finishing. Maybe price per square metre too.

I don't need twenty different things. Just the important information in one place.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever contact developers to check prices?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, I contacted a few. Because sometimes the price on the website isn't the final price.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really? What happened?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
One time, I found an apartment at a pretty good price. I called the manager, and he said that exact apartment was already reserved.

He offered me another one, but it was more expensive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh, I see. What about finishing? Was that important?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, actually, very important. Because I want to rent the apartment out, I need to know how much I'll spend before someone can move in.

If it's completely unfinished, I'll need to spend more money and time on repairs.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So would you pay more for a finished apartment?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Maybe, yeah. If the difference isn't too big.

For example, if one apartment costs 28 million without finishing, and another costs 31 million but is almost ready, I'd compare the total costs.

I don't want to buy a cheaper apartment and then find out I need to spend much more money on it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, let's talk about the building itself. How did you check where the apartment was located?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Usually, I looked at the floor plans on the developer's website. But sometimes they were confusing.

I could see the rooms, but I couldn't understand where the apartment was in the building.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And does that matter if you're going to rent it out?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. For example, if the windows face a busy road, it could be noisy. Or if the apartment is right next to another building, the view might not be great.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you visit any of the locations?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: I visited one. But most of the time, I just checked the map and pictures online.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about a 360-degree view? Would you use something like that?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, definitely. If I could look around the courtyard and see what's near the building, that would be nice.

I mean, it wouldn't replace visiting the place, but it would help me decide which buildings are worth visiting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So when you contacted developers, how did it usually go?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Mostly okay. I called them or left my phone number.

Usually, they called me back and started explaining their apartments.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Anything you didn't like?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, sometimes they kept calling after that.

Like, I just wanted to ask about one apartment, but then they started offering me different buildings.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would be a better way for you?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd prefer to send a message about a specific apartment and get an answer about that one.

I don't mind sharing my name and phone number, but I don't want to create an account just to see prices.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: By the way, what language do you usually use on these websites?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Mostly Russian. I'm just used to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was there anything you didn't understand?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, some construction terms. Like WhiteBox. I knew the word, but I wasn't sure what was actually included.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you try to find an explanation?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, I Googled it. But then I realised different developers can mean different things by it.

I think they should just show what's included. Like walls, floors, bathroom, electricity. Something simple.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, now let's look at our website. Imagine you're searching for an apartment here. What would you do first?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, okay. First, I'd probably set my budget. Then choose one-room apartments.

After that, I'd check the map because location matters a lot to me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Let's say you found a building you like. What next?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd open it, check the available apartments, and look at the prices.

Oh, and I'd probably check the floor plans too.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Now imagine you've found two apartments. How would you choose between them?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
I'd compare the prices, area, and finishing. Also, I'd check which one is closer to public transport.

If both look good, I'd probably contact the developer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything here that's confusing or missing?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Hmm, maybe I'd like to see the total price more clearly when choosing finishing.

And since I'm buying to rent out, it would be useful to see information about nearby universities or business centres.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Anything else?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Maybe the date when the price was updated. I don't want to call about an apartment that's already sold.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Last question. Imagine you could just tell an AI assistant what apartment you want, and it finds options for you. Would you use that?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, why not? I'd try it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you tell it?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Something like, "Find me a one-room apartment in Astana under 30 million, near public transport, that could be good for renting out."

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And would you trust the suggestions?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Well, not immediately. I'd still check the apartments myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What exactly would you check?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
The price, location, finishing, and maybe how much similar apartments rent for in that area.

If the AI says an apartment is a good investment, I want to know why.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you want some explanation, not just a list?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text:
Yeah, exactly. Like, don't just tell me it's good. Show me why you think it's good.

And I think comparing apartments would still be the most useful feature for me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text:
Okay, I think that's everything. Let me just check if I understood you correctly.

So, your main goal is to find an apartment that isn't too expensive and could be easy to rent out.

And the biggest problems are comparing apartments, understanding the real total price, and checking the location. Right?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, pretty much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And you'd like a website where you can compare apartments, check their surroundings, and get suggestions based on what you're looking for.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Exactly. That would save a lot of time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything else you want to add?

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Hmm, not really. Just keep the website simple. I don't want to spend half an hour trying to understand how it works.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Haha, fair enough. Thanks a lot for your time.

turns.speaker: Participant
turns.text: Yeah, no problem. Good luck with the project!
